title: Biomarker Assays for Elevated Prostate-Specific Antigen Risk Analysis -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Serum prostate-specific antigen testing is the primary method for screening and early detection of prostate cancer. This testing is known for its sensitivity but is limited by low specificity. Elevated levels of prostate-specific antigen can result from benign conditions, leading to potential overdiagnosis and unnecessary biopsies, which strain healthcare resources. Ideal biomarkers are highly sensitive and specific, easy to use, cost-effective, and approved by relevant health authorities, enhancing their use in clinical practice. This activity discusses risk-stratification biomarkers designed for lower-risk and borderline patients, typically with prostate-specific antigen levels between 4 and 10 ng/mL, and the interpretation of test results, including avoiding further invasive diagnostics for negative results, thereby reducing unnecessary procedures or diagnostic biopsies for high-risk patients.

content: This course reviews current and investigational biomarkers, including blood- and urine-based assays, and their integration into clinical practice to improve diagnostic accuracy by supplementing prostate-specific antigen testing. Participants will also gain an understanding of each biomarker's unique advantages for detecting, diagnosing, and monitoring prostate cancer, as well as risk assessment tools to support better clinical decision-making. title: Biomarker Assays for Elevated Prostate-Specific Antigen Risk Analysis -- Introduction
content: Prostate cancer ranks among the most frequently detected malignancies in males, accounting for approximately 1.4 million new cases worldwide each year. [1] This disease represents the most commonly diagnosed cancer and the second leading cause of cancer-related mortality in men, with an estimated 2.4 million cases projected for 2040, according to the National Cancer Institute (NCI). Approximately 1 in 8 men develops prostate cancer over a lifetime. Despite this high incidence, the typically indolent disease course contributes to a mortality rate of only 1 in 41 diagnosed men.

title: Biomarker Assays for Elevated Prostate-Specific Antigen Risk Analysis -- Introduction
content: One of the most effective approaches for screening, diagnosis, staging, assessment of therapeutic response, and prognostication in prostate cancer involves the use of serum or urine biomarkers for risk assessment. The NCI defines a biomarker as a biological molecule identified in blood, urine, other body fluids, or tissues that signals an abnormal process, condition, or disease. Appropriate application of biomarkers allows healthcare professionals to individualize diagnostic strategies while minimizing unnecessary diagnostic interventions and reducing the risk of overtreatment.

These biomarkers may include proteins, DNA, messenger RNA (mRNA), metabolites, prostate cancer cells or their derivatives, exosomes, or measurements of cellular processes, eg, proliferation or apoptosis. content: Approximately 66% of prostate cancer cases are diagnosed in individuals older than 65, with the average age of initial diagnosis being 66. title: Biomarker Assays for Elevated Prostate-Specific Antigen Risk Analysis -- Etiology and Epidemiology
content: Genomic evaluation has identified more than 100 genes contributing to the risk of prostatic malignancy. [4] [5] [6] About 15% to 17% of the prostate cancer population has been identified as having germline mutations. Such mutations are independent of the cancer stage. A study of multigene testing among men with prostate cancer across the United States by Giri et al concluded that 15.6% of the study population had pathogenic variations of the genes studied, including BRCA1 , BRCA2 , HOXB13 , MLH1 , MSH2 , PMS2 , MSH6 , EPCAM , ATM CHEK2 , NBN , and TP53 . [7] [8] The most commonly found pathologic gene variation identified was BRCA2 (4.5%). [7] Nicolosi et al reported that 17.2% of the study population had a pathogenic germline variant, and genomic analysis could help identify high-risk families. [9] [10] [11]

content: The Identification of Men with a Genetic Predisposition to Prostate Cancer (IMPACT) study evaluated men aged 40 to 69 with BRCA1 or BRCA2 germline mutations by screening with PSA annually and targeted biopsy if PSA greater than 3.0 ng/mL. title: Biomarker Assays for Elevated Prostate-Specific Antigen Risk Analysis -- Pathophysiology
content: Inflammation of the prostate gland, often caused by various genetic mutations, is the earliest sign of prostate cancer. This inflammation leads to oxidative damage, which causes telomeres at the ends of chromosomes to shorten, eventually initiating the development of prostate cancer. Several genes, including MYC , PTEN , NKX3.1 , and the TMPRSS2-ERG gene fusion, have been identified in the initiation and development of prostate cancer, even though no single tumor suppressor gene is primarily responsible.

title: Biomarker Assays for Elevated Prostate-Specific Antigen Risk Analysis -- Diagnostic Tests -- Prostate-specific antigen
content: PSA, a member of the kallikrein gene family, was first identified and isolated in 1979. [27] PSA is secreted by prostatic ductal and acinar epithelium and is highly organ-specific. PSA is circulated in free (fPSA) and protein-bound forms (complexed). The expression of PSA is androgen-dependent and is a crucial tool for the early detection, staging, treatment planning, and prognosis of prostate cancer. The widespread use of PSA testing in the 1990s led to increased prostate cancer diagnoses and a subsequent decline in mortality rates for this disease.

title: Biomarker Assays for Elevated Prostate-Specific Antigen Risk Analysis -- Diagnostic Tests -- Prostate-specific antigen
content: Although an excellent and sensitive biomarker, PSA is organ-specific rather than disease-specific. Prostatic basal layer and basement membrane violations allow PSA to escape prostate cells and enter the bloodstream, leading to an increase in serum PSA levels. [28] [29] This increase in serum PSA levels may occur in several prostatic pathologies, eg, benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostatitis, or prostate malignancy, or transiently with prostatic manipulation, as in prostate biopsies, prostatic massage, or urethral catheterization. [27] [30] [31] [32] [33]

title: Biomarker Assays for Elevated Prostate-Specific Antigen Risk Analysis -- Diagnostic Tests -- Prostate risk stratification biomarkers
content: The primary purpose of prostate risk stratification biomarker tests is to identify patients with a negative result who do not require further immediate testing, imaging, or biopsies. content: Clinical decision-making is enhanced by using PSA derivatives, eg, PSA density, velocity, doubling time, age-adjusted values, and, recently, different molecular derivatives. PSA velocity is the rate of change of PSA over a year, whereas PSA density is the PSA-derived computation of total PSA (tPSA) divided by prostatic volume. The PSA doubling time measures how quickly a rising PSA level doubles, gauging the rate-dependent exponential rise in serum PSA over time . These PSA-derived metrics are used for decision-making regarding prostate biopsy in an early detection setting.

title: Biomarker Assays for Elevated Prostate-Specific Antigen Risk Analysis -- Diagnostic Tests -- Human kallikrein 2 and the 4K score
content: Human kallikrein 2 (hK2) shares many similarities with PSA. They are both regulated by androgens, are proteases, and have an identical specificity for the prostate. [69] However, in contrast to PSA, hK2 is a much more potent protease and is selectively expressed in cancerous tissue, where its expression correlates with the neoplasm/s aggressiveness, degree of differentiation, and risk of biochemical recurrence. [69] Combining fPSA with hK2 has increased the cancer detection rate in the 4 to 10 ng/mL PSA range.

title: Biomarker Assays for Elevated Prostate-Specific Antigen Risk Analysis -- Diagnostic Tests -- Human kallikrein 2 and the 4K score
content: In the 4K score assay, the 4 kallikrein proteins—tPSA, fPSA, intact PSA, and hK2—are integrated. The 4K score predicts the likelihood of biopsy-positive prostate cancer when paired with clinical characteristics, including age and prior negative biopsies. This biomarker also accurately predicts cancer aggressiveness. [70] Meta-analysis has shown that the 4K test improves the predictive accuracy of biopsy by 8% to 10% and reduces the rate of unnecessary biopsies by 48% to 56%. [71] The 4K score also predicts the risk of distant metastasis even 20 years later in men with a PSA of 2 ng/mL or greater. The 4K score has been included in the NCCN prostate cancer early detection guidelines. [72]

content: Exosomes are tiny extracellular vesicles (40-150 nm) released by various cell types, including cancerous cells. They contain lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids. Prostate-derived exosomes serve as diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers as they are a source of proteins and microRNA. [81] [82] Urinary exosome analysis offers benefits, including the stability of exosomes owing to their lipid bilayer, which protects their genetic content from enzymatic degradation. No unpleasant prostatic massage is needed before collecting the sample, and the test can be performed at home with the specimen mailed directly to the laboratory by the patient, saving staff time and paperwork. Exosomal RNA and protein content may be superior to less stable, chemical, nongenetic-based biomarkers.

content: The Select MDx is an RT-PCR assay that analyzes urine specimens after DRE, along with other chemical risk factors, to facilitate early detection of prostate malignancy and decision-making regarding biopsy. This 3-gene panel assay has enhanced the identification of high-grade cancer by integrating HOXC6, TDRD1, and DLX1 mRNA levels in urine with other clinical indicators. title: Biomarker Assays for Elevated Prostate-Specific Antigen Risk Analysis -- Diagnostic Tests -- TMPRSS2-ERG gene fusions and My Prostate Score 2
content: With the discovery of gene fusions in prostate malignancy, considerable research has been performed to harness their utility as prostate cancer biomarkers. The most common gene alteration in prostate cancer is the fusion of the androgen-regulated gene transmembrane protease, serine 2 ( TMPRSS2 ), with the N-terminal-deleted ERG coding region. [109] Between 50% and 60% of patients with prostate cancer of European ancestry have this gene fusion, which results in the oncogenic activation of ERG. title: Biomarker Assays for Elevated Prostate-Specific Antigen Risk Analysis -- Testing Procedures
content: Most urinary biomarker assays are performed after prostatic manipulation (massage), except the ExoDx EPI score, which is not required. Studies have shown that a DRE can enrich urinary biomarkers and enhance yield; the first void after a DRE is obtained and analyzed. Following a prostate massage, the first 10 to 50 mL of urine voided is centrifuged at 1,000 to 2,000 rotations per minute to produce urine precipitates that may contain prostate cancer cells, cell fragments, and various biomolecules, eg, DNA, RNA, and proteins. Free proteins, DNA, RNA, other tiny molecules, and exosomes are all detected in the supernatant.

title: Biomarker Assays for Elevated Prostate-Specific Antigen Risk Analysis -- Clinical Significance
content: Serum PSA is the gold standard during initial investigation for initial prostate cancer screening and early detection. PSA as a biomarker is a sensitive tool, but its specificity is low. Various benign conditions, eg, benign prostatic hyperplasia and prostatitis, and manipulations, eg, DRE, biopsy, and catheterization, can increase PSA levels. Consequently, a diagnosis with PSA alone can lead to overdiagnosis and unwanted biopsies, adding pressure on healthcare systems and causing unnecessary patient anxiety.

title: Biomarker Assays for Elevated Prostate-Specific Antigen Risk Analysis -- Clinical Significance
content: A PSA level eliminating the risk of prostate cancer does not exist. Instead, the likelihood of prostate cancer and an aggressive disease increases as the PSA rises. Instead of using an absolute PSA level to establish if a prostate biopsy is necessary, the clinician should consider other variables, including prostate volume, inflammation, medications, patient age, life expectancy, prior PSA levels, and comorbidities.

title: Biomarker Assays for Elevated Prostate-Specific Antigen Risk Analysis -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Optimal use of risk-stratification biomarker assays for prostate cancer can significantly reduce unnecessary diagnostic procedures and treatments. The healthcare team should be familiar with implementing these assays when appropriate and help educate the patient and family when necessary or requested. The screening, diagnosis, and treatment must be individualized based on age, high-risk characteristics, comorbid conditions, life expectancy, and personal preferences. Eligible patients may be spared from such adversities by utilizing active surveillance protocols.
